newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia takes tough stance on NATO expansion.
newsitem.headline: Russia takes tough stance on NATO expansion.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin and other Russian leaders agreed on tough opposition to NATO's plans to expand eastwards on Monday and ordered a plan of action to be drawn up to prepare Moscow's response.

Yeltsin summoned Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, Kremlin chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais and security chiefs after weekend talks with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl produced no breakthrough.
"Russia's unequivocally negative position in relation to NATO's plans to expand to the East was confirmed," Yeltsin's press secretary, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, told a Kremlin briefing.

The leaders discussed ways to cooperate with NATO but also how to respond if the Western alliance goes ahead with its plans to take in former members of the Soviet bloc, which Moscow says would threaten its security.
Yeltsin ordered the foreign ministry to take responsibility for preparing a flexible response to enlargement.
"A plan of action will be worked out on Russia's position, its negative position. Consequently, action plans can be worked out for various circumstances," Yastrzhembsky said.
"NATO expansion can, after all, be multi-faceted and could involve various decisions, so Russia's position must include possible adequate steps for various scenarios."
Kohl said after meeting Yeltsin on Saturday that he hoped a "rational solution" could be reached over the enlargement issue to satisfy all sides' security concerns.
Yastrzhembsky said both sides had agreed Russia-NATO relations were "issue number one" in international relations for 1997 but made clear that progress had been insignificant.
The dispute looks set to shape Russia's foreign policy as the alliance prepares to issue membership invitations next July, with Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic heading the list.
Russia seems determined to win as many concessions as possible even if it cannot prevent enlargement.
Monday's meeting, which had not previously been announced, was the latest sign that Yeltsin is toughening his stance after his return to the Kremlin following heart surgery.

In London, Western diplomatic sources told Reuters that Yeltsin had set out demands to Kohl for a legally-binding commitment from NATO to involve Russia in formal consultations with NATO on any issue including enlargement.
Yeltsin also told Kohl there could be no expansion of NATO's military structures to new members, the sources said.
In Moscow, a recently-appointed Yeltsin aide also signalled Russia was preparing a tough reply if its demands were not met.

The aide, Sergei Shakhrai, said Russia should rethink its obligations to international arms treaties if NATO expanded eastwards and said the most effective response would be to forge ahead with a much-discussed union with Belarus.
Yastrzhembsky later played down talk of union with Belarus, which would create a border between Russia's sphere of influence and NATO's if Poland, as expected, joins the Western alliance.

One defence expert, Pavel Felgengauer of the daily newspaper Sevodnya, said Yeltsin wanted a binding agreement defining the rules of military behaviour in Europe and the right to veto any Western military build-up.
The defence ministry newspaper Krasnaya Zvezda also set out demands for a tough stance by publishing an article on Saturday outlining objections to enlargement on military grounds.
Yeltsin is due to meet French President Jacques Chirac on February 2 and British Prime Minister John Major soon. The dispute with NATO is likely to dominate both meetings.
